newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa's recovery held back by bronchitis.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa's recovery held back by bronchitis.

text.p: Doctors treating Mother Teresa said on Tuesday the revered missionary's recovery from life-saving heart surgery was being delayed by persistent respiratory problems.

But the 86-year-old nun made some progress on Tuesday against stubborn bronchitis as she recovers in hospital from heart surgery performed last month, a panel of doctors treating her at Calcutta's B.M. Birla Heart Research Centre said.
"(Her) bronchial pneumonia (is) responding to therapy, showing slight improvement today," the doctors said in a regular medical bulletin.
Dr Patricia Aubanel, an American member of the panel, said Mother Teresa has suffered from bronchitis for many years.
"She has had some bronchitis for a long time and some lung disease for a long time, even when she was a child," Dr Aubanel said. "She's been having bronchitis for the last two months."
Aubanel said the bronchitis germ was a difficult organism to treat, having built up resistance to many antibiotics given to Mother Teresa during earlier illnesses.
"Finally we found the right antibiotic for her and it seems she's trying to respond," Aubanel told reporters.

"But obviously her lungs are not as strong as they were before. Her lungs are weaker, so it takes a longer time to recuperate, she needs a lot of respiratory therapy, a lot of exercise and we're feeling for her as well," Aubanel added.

Mother Teresa underwent surgery to clear two blocked coronary arteries on November 29. She had appeared to be recovering, despite an irregular heartbeat, when long-standing kidney and lung problems complicated her recovery.
Doctors say her kidney function has since returned to normal. Her cardiac status was stable, despite her irregular heartbeat. But her body was fighting to shake off the bronchial problems.
Aubanel said the doctors hoped the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize winner would be well enough to return home for Christmas.

Mother Teresa has frequently said during the last week that she would like to return as soon as possible to her work among the poor, the sick and the terminally ill, labors which have earned her the title, the "Saint of the Gutters".
"When are you sending me home?" a clinic official quoted her as saying on Tuesday. "I'm absolutely all right," she told A.K. Chatterjee, an administrator who met her briefly.

Chatterjee said Mother Teresa seemed cheerful and was talking to colleagues from the Missionaries of Charity religious order she founded in 1948. The order's 4,500 nuns run about 456 charitable homes in 111 nations.
Mother Teresa has continued to practice taking a few steps with assistance, the doctors said.
"She spends many hours of her day praying," the medical bulletin said.
Aubanel said doctors had decided to postpone a procedure to stabilise Mother Teresa's heartbeat until she gained strength.
The doctors have warned that Mother Teresa's recovery might take a long time and she may never be as active as before.

"I'm not saying that she's going to be the way she was before," Aubanel said. "She has underlying chronic disease that we're not going to be able to take care of, but she's going to need a lot of care."
